title: Bendōwa 2 - For Authentic Seekers
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The main teaching of this Soto Zen dharma talk is that true freedom and peace can be found by letting go of our ego's need for external validation and instead embracing our natural state of being. Dogen's experiences as a monk, including his time in China and his focus on transmitting the true teachings of Zen, emphasize the importance of establishing practice without expectation or attachment to enlightenment. By doing so, we can cultivate acceptance of who we are and find peace beyond conscious experience, allowing us to live more freely and authentically.

sentences.text: **Nomon Tim Burnett:** Good evening everybody.
I want to especially welcome Chris back.
Caught her at a good moment there, blowing her nose.
Chris was just at Upaya Zen Center for a three week residential practice period led by Norman and Kathy Fischer together.
**Participant:** Did they just trade off giving talks and stuff like that?
How did they do it together?
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** They did trade off, and they did it together, and it was quite interesting.
Sometimes it would be Kathy by herself and Norman by himself, and sometimes it would be tag team, bouncing things around, and both answering the same questions from their individual points of view.
That's a great thing to do if you ever get a chance to do a practice period or be at a Zen training place where you can live.
It's a nice thing to do, but there's nothing wrong with what we're doing.
That's what I've gradually realized.
Not to feel like what we're doing here is incomplete and one day you'll get the real deal.
There's no real deal.
Sorry.
It's all the real deal.
Same thing.
So, continuing our conversation about our great Zen ancestor Eihei Dogen.
Like most of the great religious geniuses of world history, he started really early and he also died pretty early.
Most of those guys don't live that long.
And he had real challenges early in life.
His mother died when he was just seven years old.
He later wrote about watching the incense smoke at her funeral, that this was a profound moment, some sense of impermanence.
He was raised mostly by his elder half brother.
His father was some kind of high class aristocratic person.
I'm not sure if anything is really known about him.

But it's clear that the family had some resources, because it must be that Dogen as a young man received a really good education, given his later ability to write and to reference classical literature of Japan and China, and just the wild stuff he could do with language.
It's clear he must have gotten a really good education, even though probably his mother was not married to his father and he was probably a kind of low caste person in a high caste society.
And he ordained really young.
He left what little family he had to become a monk when he was 13.
The dominant Buddhism of the day was a school of Buddhism which still exists, called Tendai Buddhism.
So at the age of 13 he went to the ordination platform at Mount Hiei, which I've been to.
It's just this dark little old wood building, but somehow there's a certain majesty up on top of this mountain, surrounded by these really big Japanese cedar trees, enormous trees.
In other places that we went in Japan when I was there, you didn't really see very many big trees.
It's all rice and densely inhabited, but there are really big trees on Mount Hiei.
Tendai Buddhism, to our eyes, I think would seem sort of formulaic, sort of rote.
One book I have summarized Tendai Buddhism of that time as a synthesis of many Chinese teachings of esoteric Buddhism, the Buddhism of the Shingon sect and the Vinaya school.
The primary work of monks was to memorize and copy texts and perform elaborate rituals.
Meditation was not a very big part of it, not what would look like meditation to us.
When I was on Mount Hiei with the group a couple of years ago, I don't know if this is for visitors or if they've always arranged it that way, but you could look down into one of the buildings.
I don't know if there's a big opening or a big window or something.

And we could watch this monk doing an elaborate fire ceremony, a little fire in front of him, and he was arranging the wood in a certain way and moving things around and making offerings and ringing bells and all these [unclear: "mood rides"].
[unclear: "And he could tell us this kind of thing"] that must have taken years and years to learn.
And he was just sitting there doing it.
I'm sure, like most monastic situations, it was very busy, and probably the young monks also did the scut work too, in addition to being expected to keep up with their studies.
Just learning about Tendai Buddhism itself must have been a full-time job.

But I suspect that young Dogen, who was from the get-go a hyper-motivated and hard-working and determined person, probably stayed up late into the night studying Buddhism, even beyond the request of his monastic teachers at Mount Hiei.
The guy was really driven.

The fascinating thing about this essay we're looking at, the second essay he wrote after returning from China, called Bendowa, is that basically his conclusion after 30-something years of intensive practice is that the main thing to do is to let go: to let go of striving and immerse yourself in your original nature.
So let's reread the first three paragraphs of the text.
I won't say too much more about them.
If you weren't here last week, you can listen to the recording and then we'll go on.
And by the way, I also brought photocopies.
I put them on the back table there, to take with you and read at home if you'd like to study this, or you could look at them here while I'm speaking.
I'm not sure which would be better.
It's a photocopy of a book with really small type, so it's a little bit hard to read if you're in the situation I'm in here.
I think I'm good, thank you.
Okay, so this is the essay Bendowa, written by Dogen after he journeyed to China and back.
He wrote:
*Buddha Tathagatas all have a wonderful means, an unexcelled way, free from human agency, for transmitting the wondrous Dharma and realizing supreme and complete awakening.
That this means is only passed on from Buddha to Buddha without deviation is due to the Jijuyu Samadhi, which is its touchstone.*
Breaking briefly: Jijuyu Samadhi is a kind of concentration, a kind of way of being where everything takes care of itself.
Literally it means self-actualizing blissful concentration.
We'll say more about that in a minute.
*To disport oneself, to play freely in this Samadhi, the right entrance is proper sitting in Zazen.
The Dharma is amply present in every person, but without practice it is not manifested.
Without realization it is not attained.
It is not a question of one or many.
Let loose of it and it fills your hands.
It is not bounded vertically or horizontally.
Speak it and it fills your mouth.
Within this Dharma, Buddhas dwell everlastingly, leaving no perceptions in any sphere or direction.
All living beings use it unceasingly with no sphere or direction appearing in their perceptions.
The negotiation of the way with concentrated effort that I now teach makes myriad Dharmas exist in realization and, in transcending realization, practices a total reality.
Then, when you're over the barrier, with all bonds cast off, you are no longer affected by such segmented distinctions.*
Got all that?
So, the book was written, I don't know, five years ago, also a collection of talks and essays by American Zen teachers on pieces of Dogen's writing, called Receiving the Marrow.
The book was edited by Edo Frances Carney, who is the [unclear: "avid"] of Olympia Zen Center, Olympia, Washington.
And Edo Kassan will be here on Sunday.
So she's partly responsible for [unclear: "the Christian's book"].

The first essay in this book, which is called "Receiving the Marrow," by a teacher named, I don't know this person, so I've got to look at her name again, a person named Tejo Munik, is on the Bendowa.
So let's hear what Tejo Munik has to say about this Jijuyu Samadhi that Dogen is trying to tell us about here.
Okay, so Tejo Sensei wrote:
*Samadhi is usually translated as concentration, but this word can be misleading.
Concentration is often understood as something we do with our minds, in this case thinking we can use our minds as the primary source of our awakening.
This is the opposite of what Dogen is trying to express here.*
I'll read that part again.

So it's misleading because we think of concentration as something we do with our minds, and in this case we think we can use our minds as the primary source of our awakening, which we think that, right?
I can only just figure this thing out.
Maybe it's like shutting off my mind, maybe it's thinking about things the right way, maybe it's reading the right stuff, something, but it's like me, me, me, me.
So he says, no, that's not what he's talking about.
She goes on:
*The experience of the joy of Samadhi was through dance.

Before I met Katagiri Roshi and began to throw myself into Zazen practice, I was studying dance and had experienced the letting go that comes when one completely gives oneself over to the form and to the teacher.
In order to perform a dance, one has to first learn the steps.
After the steps are somewhat mastered, the flow of the dance begins to emerge, and at this point resistance arises.
One doesn't yet have a total picture of the dance, but through the steps and the flow, there's a sense of accomplishment, which seems to be enough, and then weariness sets in.
And there doesn't seem to be anything else to do.
Maybe there's a feeling that going further is beyond the ability of the dancer.
You feel really stuck.
So the next part of the process is you just continue dancing.
You go beyond the resistance and exhaust it.
At that point, the dancer becomes the dance, and is danced by the dance.
There is no longer any effort, and the dance is perfect.
Although my experience of Samadhi through dance was wondrous, at the time I didn't recognize the process that was happening.
I didn't even see it as a process.
I simply saw it as something that happens sometimes when I danced.*
*One of the benefits of studying with a teacher is that by trusting and submitting to the teacher's guidance, letting go happens.
To follow an aspiration is an important component, but if we do it alone, we have only our own experiences to draw from.
And because our experiences are limited, it's easy to go around in circles.
We look at and we judge what we're doing, seeing it only from one perspective, our own.
But a teacher allows us to enter into the process in ways we haven't imagined, and then nudges us to continue just when we think we can't go on.
The teacher can help us get beyond our resistance.
So Samadhi is a kind of concentration in which you absolutely merge.
There's no distinction between you and what you're doing.
Sometimes Samadhi is translated as one-pointedness.
This means the ability to stay in touch with and return to the source of awakening.
The source of awakening is reality itself, simply described as impermanence and no-self.
Impermanence is the movement of life, the changing, exchanging, and rearranging that everything in life is doing in every moment.
It is simultaneously death and birth moment by moment.
No-self describes our good, true relationship with life.
There's not a definable self existing separate from everything else in life.
What we call myself is part of and dependent on the life of all things.
This is true of everything.
So when one thing changes, everything changes.
The movement is constant and that is what we awaken to when we let go of our ideas.
And that is what Dogen is talking about.*
So that helps, huh?
Jijuyu Samadhi is like losing yourself in the dance and letting the dance take care of you.
So Dogen goes on now with some storytelling after introducing his topic.
You can tell a little bit of the back story.
He wrote:
*After the religious mind awoke in me, awakening the desire to seek the way, I visited many religious teachers throughout the country.
I chanced to encounter the priest Myozen of Keninji.
Swiftly past the frost and flowers of the nine years I studied with him, during that time I learned something of the manner of the Rinzai Zen school.
As the chief disciple of the patriarch Isai, it was Myozen alone who genuinely transmitted the supreme Buddha Dharma.
None of Isai's other followers could compare with him.*

So after being some couple of years at Mount Hiei studying with the Tendai people, he heard about this other temple, which is in fact not a Zen temple yet, but a Tendai temple also called Keninji, which is right in Kyoto, just across the river from the main part of Kyoto.
The previous teacher there, named Isai, got interested in Zen somehow, and he went to China.
So Dogen wasn't the first of these guys to go to China.
Isai actually went to China twice.
He was starting to include some Zen techniques and Zen thinking and Zen practices, Zen sensibility, into what was happening at this other monastery, Keninji.
And then he probably had many students.
One of his students, this guy named Myozen, really liked the Zen stuff.
So that's why Dogen says he's the best.
Dogen's a little sectarian, you know.
Zen school's the best way.
So anyway, somehow, I don't know how, Dogen got attracted to this and moved to Keninji and studied there for nine years.
And then Myozen got the idea he needed to go to China too, and try to learn something of what his teacher, Isai, had learned there.
And by the way, one of the surviving writings we have from Isai, and I don't think there are many, but one I know about is all about tea.
He's really into tea.
He brought tea back.
I don't know, maybe he must have had tea in Japan, but he brought back some really good tea from China and was telling all the monks.
He wrote an essay about tea.
Like, you should drink lots of tea.
Anyway, I can give you the tea essay if you want.
So Dogen goes on:
*After that, I proceeded to the great Song China.*
So Song is the Song dynasty.
*So I proceeded to China where I visited leading priests of the [unclear: "Lin She"] region.
And learned of the characteristics of the five Zen gates.
Finally, I practiced under Zen master [unclear: "Lu Xing"] at Mount [unclear: "Tiaipai"].
And there I resolved the one great matter of Zen practice for my entire life.
Then, when I returned home in the first year of the [unclear: "Shating"] period of the Song, my thoughts turned to preaching the Dharma for the salvation of my fellow beings.
And it was as though I'd taken a heavy burden upon my shoulders.*
Pausing there.
There are many important stories about what happened to Dogen and Myozen both when they went to China.

Several of the most important stories are actually retold, not in this text, but in Dogen's instructions to the cook text, the Tenzo Kyokun, which we're going to study, and then we'll really work with it more than these talks.
We're going to study that on the May 20th, 21st study weekend.
Dogen also writes a bunch about his time in China in a text called the Hokyoki, which I mentioned last week, which seems to be a journal of what happened in China for Dogen.
But it was not discovered until after he died, and some scholars are a little uncertain whether it's for sure he wrote it or not.
These things happened 900 years ago, so who knows really.
But for sure Dogen went to China, that's clear.
And he learned a lot when he was there and connected with this one teacher.
This teacher, [unclear: "Ru Qing"], is not a particularly famous or important teacher, actually.
And the same is true of Suzuki Roshi, so there's a parallel there.
Suzuki Roshi became very well known in America.
His teachings in English, written in Zen mind beginner's mind, and then the book that came later, not only so, later got translated into Japanese and received a little interest in Japan.
But while he was in Japan, he was a very important minor temple priest and we paid attention to him.
So similarly, this particular abbot wasn't a particularly important teacher in China, but somehow just the right teacher for Dogen.
And that, I think, is really characteristic of our way of thinking about things.
It's really just a matter of finding the right teacher.
They don't have to be famous or important or brilliant.
They just have to be the person who holds the space for you and helps you see something about yourself.
Later we'll get into some of the stories of what happened with Dogen while he was in China.
This next part has a sweetness to it and a little tinge of sadness.
He gets back and he's had this big, big experience, this epic time in China, and not without difficulty.
The journey apparently was very perilous.
The boats were barely up for getting across the South China Sea.
In one of the stories on the way back, the ship almost sank in a storm.
And he was there about three years.
Towards the end of the first year, Myozen, who he went there with, the teacher from Kenninji, got sick and died.
So the guy he went there to study alongside died.
And of course much of Dogen's family had died.
He was disconnected from them.
Eisai, the importer of Zen to this temple, had also died when Dogen was 15.
So he's alone.
He's back at Kenninji.
Myozen is gone.
He has this feeling maybe he's the only one who gets this way of thinking about practice.
And after a couple of years he moves to an abandoned temple outside of town that nobody really cared about.
And now he's writing about his time then:
*It was as though I'd taken on a heavy burden on my shoulders.

Nevertheless, in order to await the time when I can work vigorously to this end, and unburden myself of this desire to spread the Dharma far and wide, I am for the time being living like a cloud or like a water plant, drifting without any fixed abode, attempting to transmit through my actions the way of life followed by outstanding Zen masters of the past.
But there will be those of no concern for gain or glory, there will be authentic religious seekers whose desire for the way takes precedence over all else.
They will be led vainly astray by mistaken teachers, and the right understanding will be arbitrarily obscured from them.*
So watch out for that.
*They will become needlessly drunk with their own delusion and immersed forever in a world of illusion.
How can the true seed of wisdom be expected to quicken and grow within such seekers?
How will they ever reach the moment of attainment?
As I am now committed to the wandering life, to what mountain, to what river will they proceed to find me?

It's with a sense of pity for the plight of such people that I now write down, for those who would learn to practice the way, the customs and standards of the great Zen monasteries of [unclear: "Songqian"], that I saw with my own eyes and have learned, and the profound teachings of their masters that I have succeeded to and follow and transmit.
I want such seekers to know the right Buddha Dharma.
Here are its true essentials.*
It's a little personal interlude from Dogen.
And it's a great mythic story, his story, like so many great stories: the solo voyager, the hero bringing back something precious, going off to find something and returning home.
And what he found, he's concerned, is so precious that others won't even recognize it.
It's like you go off and have a really powerful experience at retreat here and you're like, wow!
And you get back home and your spouse hands you the baby and says, could you do those dishes?
Not everybody's going to get it in that certain way, right?
Dogen's sensibility, as oddly expressed as it is in his many, many, many writings, was greatly appreciated by Suzuki Roshi.
But as I mentioned last week, it wasn't really continuously handed down exactly from person to person to person.
Maybe it was in some lived way.
But these written teachings actually got set aside and more or less forgotten about until the 18th and 19th century.
For one thing, there wasn't a whole lot of printing press going on or very many copies.
But for another thing, they were revered as important spiritual objects, the actual written documents, as well they should be.
And so what do you do with a revered spiritual document?
You hide it away.
You hide it away somewhere safe.
All the monasteries have treasure houses.
On our trip to Japan, we went to a small monastery outside of Eiheiji, the big monastery that Dogen founded.

In their treasure house, which they had not too long ago redone like a little museum with air conditioning and stuff, so stuff would stop degrading, they had the famous portrait of Dogen, the original portrait.
Suzuki Roshi had his own quirky way of expressing these same ideas, the same sense of a samadhi in which life deeply takes care of itself.
The dance dances you.
So I just wanted to share with you a little bit of one of his many expressions of this.
This was the first important Buddhist book for me, really, Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind.
And maybe like you're experiencing with Dogen, it's a little hard to understand, but you feel something.
You sense something.
I used to carry this around and randomly open it up and read a few pages.
I think if someone had said to me after I closed the book, so Tim, what did you just read?
I would say, ah, I don't know.
But I'd feel something.
I'd feel moved in some way.
I had a copy that I carried around in a ziplock bag everywhere I went.
So here's a little bit from Suzuki Roshi, some other expression of this [unclear: "Jujusamani"], this self-fulfilling, joyous concentration of just being alive.
He wrote, or he said, actually, these were all transcribed talks that got cleaned up a bit:
*We should establish our practice where there is no practice and there is no enlightenment.*
Right?
You're already like, okay.
*As long as we practice zazen in the area where there is practice and enlightenment, there's no chance to make peace for ourselves.
In other words, we must firmly believe in our own true nature.
Our true nature is beyond our conscious experience.
It is only in our conscious experience that we find practice and enlightenment, good and bad.
But whether or not we have the experience of our true nature, what exists there beyond consciousness actually exists, and it is there that we have to establish the foundation of our practice.*
So this is very much Dogen's understanding too.
He goes on, but let's just stick with this one paragraph.
That's enough.
So let's think about this.
We should establish our practice where there is no practice or enlightenment.
In other words, where there's no idea separate from me, separate from you, that there's something called practice and enlightenment.
As long as we practice in the area where there is practice and enlightenment, where there is this idea, there's no chance to make peace.
We're always trying to get something else.
In other words, we must firmly believe, so there's some faith here, firmly believe in our own true nature.
And yet, and yet, and yet, our true nature is beyond our conscious experience.
Conscious experience means the thinking about stuff, our self-conscious experience.
This and this and this and this.
I'm me.
You're you.
This is what's going on.
I'm grouchy.
I'm happy.
I wish this was different, and so on and so forth.
So our true nature is beyond what we can experience with that mind.
It's only, and yet another and yet, it's only in our conscious experience that we find practice and enlightenment, good and bad.
Whether or not we have the experience of our true nature, what exists there beyond consciousness actually exists.
So it's beyond what we can quite think about, but don't worry.
It really is there.
It really is something.
And it is there that we establish the foundation of our practice.
So this is another way of talking about this [unclear: "GGU Samadhi"].
I'm dancing the dance.
But it's not that there's not some practice.
It's not that there's not some feeling for life.
It's only that we can't get there by making it happen.
We can't get there in the self-conscious way.
And the great boon and the great benefit of this is if we can let go of some other attainment, some practice outside of me, then you know what else we're letting go of?
This persistent and deep idea, this fixed view, that we're not good enough.
That we're incomplete.
That we're not yet awake.
That we need something outside of what we already are and already have.
So that's my little talk on Bendowa Part 2.
Remember, if you want to read this at home, I've made photocopies.
We'll just continue plugging away at it.
We'll do another talk next week, and then Andrea's going to give a talk, and then another talk the week after that.
And then after you're around, we'll have a weekend on another Dogen text.
I wanted to do two somewhat contrasting Dogen texts.
This one is about his relationship to this understanding and expression of his philosophy.
He's opening his salvo really on what his philosophy is about all this.
And the one we're going to look at on the weekend, the instructions to the cook, is also all that, but it has some nice hands-on practical things.
Like how you actually do this with your hands, in the kitchen, in your life.
Alright.
Thanks for listening.
The other piece too is that on the weekend we have a lot more time to interact, so we'll do activities and have conversations and discussions.
In these talks there's not so much time.
And maybe the homework assignment, the take-home, might be: what are the ways in which with my mind I separate myself from some other thing that I think I'm supposed to be?
Some other thing I think I'm supposed to understand.
And can I notice, and not then immediately use your mind to beat yourself up?
Like, you dummy, you already have that.
That doesn't help.
We just notice that.
We just study that as part of our practice.
This persistent, persistent desire to get something else, to be someone else.
What if one day we fully accepted who we are?
That would be a good day.
Alright.
